questions.question: Which parts of the human ear are caused to vibrate by incoming sound waves?
options: Only the outer ear flap and the ear canal
The eardrum, tiny bones within the ear, and the cochlea
The auditory nerve and the brain tissue
The outer ear and the auditory canal only

questions.question: What is the role of the specialised cells inside the cochlea?
options: To direct sound waves from the air into the auditory canal
To amplify sound vibrations mechanically before they reach the eardrum
To sense vibrations and send electrical signals along a nerve to the brain
To block out high-frequency noises to prevent damage

questions.question: How does the brain create the sensation of hearing a sound?
options: By physically vibrating at the same frequency as the sound wave
By receiving electrical signals from the ear through a nerve
By pumping fluid directly into the cochlea
By reflecting sound waves back to the eardrum

questions.question: What is the range of sound frequencies that human ears can detect, and which range are they most sensitive to?
options: 20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 2–5 kHz
10 Hz to 10 kHz, being most sensitive to 1–2 kHz
50 Hz to 50 kHz, being most sensitive to 5–10 kHz
20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 10–15 kHz

questions.question: What are sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz and above 20 kHz called, respectively?
options: Ultrasound and infrasound
Megasound and microsound
Infrasound and ultrasound
Hypersound and hyposound

questions.question: When a sound wave travels through the air, how do the air particles move?
options: They travel continuously forwards from the source to the listener's ear
They vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel, without travelling forwards
They vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
They spin in small circles and move slowly backwards

questions.question: Why is sound classified as a longitudinal wave?
options: Because the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Because the direction of vibration is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
Because it can only travel through very long distances
Because it does not require a medium to travel through

questions.question: Why do sound waves travel faster in solids and liquids compared to gases?
options: Because solids and liquids have higher temperatures than gases
Because the particles are very close together, so vibrations are easily passed on
Because sound waves only consist of transverse vibrations in gases
Because gas particles block the passage of sound waves

questions.question: Why does sound travel even faster in solids than in liquids?
options: Because solids contain larger air gaps between their particles
Because the strong forces between particles in a solid mean vibrations travel faster
Because solids are colder than liquids
Because particles in a solid are free to move around and carry the sound

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the speed of sound in different media?
options: It is about 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids, and faster still in solids
It is fastest in air, slower in liquids, and slowest in solids
It is about 1500 m/s in air, 340 m/s in liquids, and slowest in solids
It is the same in all materials because sound speed is constant

questions.question: What causes an echo to occur?
options: Sound waves absorbing completely into a soft, carpeted surface
Sound waves reflecting from hard surfaces, travelling back, and being heard again
Sound waves refracting as they pass from air into water
Sound waves vibrating the air particles in a circular path

questions.question: An echo from a distant wall is heard 2 seconds after a sound is made. If the distance to the wall is 340 metres (making the total travel distance 680 metres), which equation would you use to find the speed of the sound wave?
options: speed = distance + time
speed = distance × time
speed = distance ÷ time
speed = time ÷ distance

questions.question: Why is it better to measure longer distances and times when designing an experiment to measure the speed of sound?
options: It ensures the sound wave changes frequency as it travels
It makes the sound travel faster, which is easier to record
Any measurement errors will make up a smaller proportion of the total measurements
It eliminates the effect of reflection entirely

questions.question: How is ultrasound used to create images of structures inside the human body?
options: It heats up different tissues to different temperatures to show them on a thermal camera
It reflects from the boundaries between different tissues
It passes straight through all tissues and is captured on an X-ray plate
It damages unwanted cells so that healthy cells stand out

questions.question: Why are water waves described as transverse waves?
options: The direction of oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer
The direction of oscillation is at 90° to the direction of energy transfer
The waves cannot reflect off hard barriers
The wave does not transfer any energy as it moves

questions.question: What occurs during wave superposition when two waves pass through each other?
options: The waves will always bounce off each other and reverse their directions
The waves can 'add up' or 'cancel out'
One wave will always absorb the other wave's energy completely
Both waves immediately stop vibrating and disappear

questions.question: What is the amplitude of a water wave?
options: The total distance a water particle travels horizontally in one second
The greatest distance water moves above and below the rest position
The distance from one wave crest to the very next wave crest
The speed at which the wave crest moves across the surface
